wars.name: War with Lars Porsenna and the Tarquins
wars.outcome: Porsenna probably captured Rome but his power in Latium collapsed after his son's defeat at Aricia (c. 504); the Tarquins failed to return.
wars.summary: The wars of the first years of the Republic, in which the exiled Tarquins enlisted Veii, Tarquinii and Lars Porsenna of Clusium against Rome.
wars.detail: Roman tradition turned the war into a series of patriotic legends (Brutus at the Silva Arsia, Horatius at the bridge, Mucius Scaevola, Cloelia) and a dignified peace. Tacitus' 'dedita urbe' and Pliny's iron-ban treaty reveal a Roman capitulation. The decisive event was not Roman: the Latin and Cumaean victory at Aricia ended Clusine ambitions. Some scholars (Alföldi, Cornell) see Porsenna as acting for himself rather than for Tarquin, as one of several Etruscan condottieri contesting Rome.

phases.t: Veii and Tarquinii back the Tarquins (Silva Arsia)
Porsenna's attack and occupation of Rome
Arruns Porsenna defeated at Aricia

wars.name: First Latin War
wars.outcome: Roman victory at Lake Regillus; Foedus Cassianum (493) establishes an equal alliance between Rome and the Latin League.
wars.summary: The war in which the Latin League, led by Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum and supporting the exiled Tarquinius, challenged Rome's claim to hegemony in Latium.
wars.detail: The Regillus narrative is epic and the outcome was probably less one-sided than Roman tradition claims: the Foedus Cassianum treats Rome as one partner and the League as the other, sharing booty and command. Rome's regal hegemony over Latium, asserted in the 509 Carthage treaty, was replaced by alliance, which held for a century and a half against the Volsci and Aequi.

phases.t: Latin mobilisation and battle of Lake Regillus
Negotiation of the Foedus Cassianum

wars.name: Volscian Wars
wars.outcome: Roman conquest of the Volscian lands in the Pontine plain and the Monti Lepini; Antium a citizen colony (338), Privernum taken (329).
wars.summary: A century and a half of intermittent warfare with the Volsci, Oscan-speaking highlanders who descended into southern Latium around 500 and took Antium, Satricum, Velitrae, Circeii and the Pontine plain.
wars.detail: The early phase (495-430s) saw the Volsci on the offensive (the Coriolanus legend preserves the memory). Rome and the Latins answered with joint colonies (Signia, Norba, Velitrae, Antium 467, Ardea 442, Circeii, Satricum 385, Setia 382) and the Hernican alliance. After the Gallic sack the Volsci revived, but by the 350s Rome controlled the Pontine plain (tribus Pomptina 358). Volscian cities fought with the Latins in 340-338; Privernum's revolt in 330-329 was the last.

phases.t: Volscian offensives and Roman-Latin colonies
Roman counter-offensive (Anxur 406)
Post-sack resurgence; Satricum and Antium; Pontine tribes
Final revolts; Antium and Privernum

wars.name: Aequian Wars
wars.outcome: Aequi defeated on the Algidus (431) and annihilated in 304; Latin colonies at Alba Fucens and Carseoli.
wars.summary: Recurrent warfare with the Aequi of the upper Anio and Turano valleys, whose raids through the Algidus pass threatened the Alban Hills and Tusculum through the 5th century.
wars.detail: Annalistic narratives of yearly Aequian incursions are formulaic, but the turning point of 431 (A. Postumius Tubertus on the Algidus) is credible, as are the colonies at Labici (418) and the capture of Bolae. The final destruction of 304, in which 31 towns were stormed in 50 days, was one of the most brutal episodes of Rome's conquest of Italy.

phases.t: Aequian raids on Latium; Algidus battles (458)
Roman offensive after Algidus 431; Labici and Bolae
Destruction of the Aequi

wars.name: First Veientine War
wars.outcome: Forty-year truce after the Fabian disaster at the Cremera and Veientine seizure of the Janiculum.
wars.summary: War with Veii for control of the right bank of the lower Tiber and the salt route, remembered chiefly for the Fabian clan's private war and annihilation at the Cremera.
wars.detail: Veii, 15 km north of Rome with a territory of comparable size, was Rome's natural rival: it controlled Fidenae and the right bank of the Tiber, while Rome sought the salt pans at the river mouth.

phases.t: Raids and battles
Fabian fort on the Cremera and its destruction
Veientines on the Janiculum; truce

wars.name: Second Veientine War (War of Fidenae)
wars.outcome: Rome captured and destroyed Fidenae (426); twenty-year truce with Veii.
wars.summary: Fidenae's defection to Lars Tolumnius of Veii led to war, the spolia opima of Cossus, and the destruction of Fidenae, giving Rome the whole left bank of the lower Tiber.
wars.detail: The murder of Roman envoys at Fidenae (statues of them stood on the Rostra) and the date of Cossus' spolia opima are the best-known problems. Livy's narrative contains doublets of two Fidenate revolts.

phases.t: Revolt of Fidenae; Tolumnius killed
Second revolt and destruction of Fidenae

wars.name: Third Veientine War
wars.outcome: Veii captured and destroyed by Camillus (396); its territory annexed, nearly doubling the ager Romanus; Capena (395) and Falerii (394) submit.
wars.summary: The 'ten-year' siege of Veii, Rome's first great war of conquest, financed by the introduction of military pay and tribute.
wars.detail: The war was transformative: year-round service, army pay (stipendium) and property tax (tributum), six consular tribunes per year, a massive land distribution in seven-iugera lots and four new tribes (387). The other Etruscan cities did not intervene, perhaps because Veii had adopted kingship (Livy) or because they were pressed by the Gauls in the north.

phases.t: Siege begins; stipendium introduced
Reverses; Capenates and Faliscans aid Veii; Alban lake prodigy
Fall of Veii; surrender of Capena and Falerii

wars.name: Gallic invasion and sack of Rome
wars.outcome: Roman defeat at the Allia, sack of the city and siege of the Capitol; the Gauls departed with a ransom of 1,000 pounds of gold.
wars.summary: The Senonian Gauls under Brennus, after besieging Clusium, routed the Romans at the Allia and sacked Rome; the Capitol held out for seven months.
wars.detail: Varronian date 390; Polybius and Greek synchronisms give 387/386. The episode was the trauma of early Roman history and one of the first Roman events known to the Greeks (Aristotle, Heraclides Ponticus, Theopompus). Camillus' victory is a fiction; Polybius says the Gauls left because the Veneti attacked their homeland, Diodorus and Strabo credit Caere with defeating them on their return.

phases.t: Siege of Clusium; Fabian envoys fight
Allia (18 July), sack, siege of the Capitol, ransom

wars.name: Gallic incursions of 367-349
wars.outcome: Gallic raids repulsed; peace with the Gauls (c. 331) kept for 30 years.
wars.summary: Recurring Gallic raids into Latium after the sack, remembered for the single combats of Manlius Torquatus (361) and Valerius Corvus (349) and the victories at Pedum (358) and in the Pomptine territory (349).
wars.detail: Polybius' sober account (2.18) reports only a few incursions in which the Romans initially did not dare engage, then did, and the Gauls withdrew; Livy multiplies battles. Some bands may have been mercenaries of Dionysius I or II of Syracuse moving between Apulia and Latium.

phases.t: Raids on the Alban Hills and the Anio
Pedum, Pomptine battles

wars.name: War with Tarquinii, Caere and Falerii
wars.outcome: Hundred-year truce with Caere (353); forty-year truces with Tarquinii and Falerii (351).
wars.summary: War with the southern Etruscan cities, notable for the sacrifice of 307 Roman prisoners at Tarquinii (358) and Rome's execution of 358 Tarquinian nobles in reprisal (354).
wars.detail: The first plebeian dictator, C. Marcius Rutilus, repelled an Etruscan raid to the Tiber salt-works (356). The Elogia Tarquiniensia may preserve the Etruscan side of this war.

phases.t: Tarquinian victory and Roman counterattack
Caere and Tarquinii sue for truces

wars.name: First Samnite War
wars.outcome: Roman victories in Campania; treaty with the Samnites renewed (341), leaving the Sidicini to the Samnites.
wars.summary: Short war triggered by the Campanians' appeal to Rome against Samnite attack, fought in Campania (Mount Gaurus, Saticula, Suessula).
wars.detail: Its historicity has been doubted (Adcock, Beloch) because Rome made peace on terms abandoning its new friends; most now accept a limited war (Salmon, Oakley). Its importance was to bring Rome into Campania, the richest region of Italy, and to set Rome and the Samnite League on a collision course.

phases.t: Deditio of Capua; battles of Gaurus, Saticula, Suessula
Mutiny of the Campanian garrison; peace

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 283-392

wars.name: Latin War (Second Latin War)
wars.outcome: Roman victory; dissolution of the Latin League and the settlement of 338.
wars.summary: The revolt of the Latins, Campanians, Volsci and Sidicini, who demanded equality (one consul and half the Senate to be Latin), and its suppression in battles at Vesuvius, Trifanum, Pedum and the Astura.
wars.detail: Usually called simply 'the Latin War'. Rome fought with Samnite support against its former allies. The settlement of 338 created the graded system of citizens, half-citizens, Latin colonies and allies that underpinned all later expansion.

phases.t: Vesuvius and Trifanum; Decius' devotio
Pedum and Astura; Latin surrender; settlement

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 405-571

wars.name: Second Samnite War (Great Samnite War)
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Samnites renew the old treaty (304); Rome holds Campania, the Liris valley and northern Apulia, ringed by colonies and the Via Appia.
wars.summary: Twenty-two-year struggle for central and southern Italy, begun over Neapolis and Fregellae, notorious for the Caudine Forks (321) and Lautulae (315), and won by a strategy of encirclement with colonies, alliances in Apulia and a military road.
wars.detail: The Romans were humiliated at the Caudine Forks and probably kept the Caudine peace until 316. From 315-314 they recovered, planted colonies at Luceria, Suessa, Pontiae, Saticula, Interamna and Fregellae, built the Via Appia, and fought a second front in Etruria (311-308). The war forged the manipular legion, the four-legion army and the system of prorogued commands.

phases.t: Neapolis; Imbrinium; Caudine Forks
Caudine peace; consolidation in Apulia and Campania
Lautulae; Campanian and Ausonian revolts crushed; colonies; Via Appia
Etruscan front; Bovianum; Hernican revolt; peace

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vols. II-III

wars.name: Etruscan War of 311-308
wars.outcome: Roman victories at Sutrium, Perusia and Lake Vadimon; thirty-year truces with Perusia, Cortona and Arretium; forty-year truce with Tarquinii (308).
wars.summary: Etruscan cities, their truce with Rome expiring, besieged Sutrium; Fabius Rullianus responded by crossing the Ciminian forest into central Etruria.
wars.detail: Effectively a second front of the Second Samnite War. Fabius' march demonstrated that Rome could project force deep into Etruria.

phases.t: Siege of Sutrium; Ciminian forest; Perusia; Vadimon
Truces; Umbrian campaign (Mevania)

scholarship: Harris, Rome in Etruria and Umbria (1971) 49-61

wars.name: Third Samnite War
wars.outcome: Roman victory at Sentinum (295) and Aquilonia (293); Samnites sue for peace (290); Curius Dentatus conquers the Sabines and Praetuttii.
wars.summary: The decisive war for Italy, in which the Samnites under Gellius Egnatius forged a coalition with Etruscans, Umbrians and Gauls that Rome broke at Sentinum.
wars.detail: Rome fielded perhaps six legions at once and settled the issue with colonies at Minturnae, Sinuessa, Venusia (291) and Hadria (289). After 290 Roman territory and alliances stretched from the Tyrrhenian to the Adriatic.

phases.t: Lucanian appeal; Scipio Barbatus; Tifernum
Coalition; Camerinum; Sentinum
Aquilonia; Venusia; Sabine conquest; peace

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005)

wars.name: War with the Senones and Boii
wars.outcome: Senones expelled and their land annexed (colony at Sena Gallica); Boii and Etruscans crushed at Lake Vadimon (283); peace with the Boii for 45 years.
wars.summary: After the Senones destroyed a Roman army at Arretium and murdered Roman envoys, Rome annexed the ager Gallicus and defeated the Boii and Etruscans in two campaigns.
wars.detail: Polybius' account (2.19-20) is the most reliable. The Roman annexation of Senonian land was unprecedented in its thoroughness and had long-term consequences in the Gallic war of 225.

phases.t: Arretium disaster; envoys murdered
Senones expelled; Vadimon
Second defeat of the Boii; peace

wars.name: Pyrrhic War (Tarentine War)
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Pyrrhus leaves Italy (275); Tarentum surrenders (272); Rome master of peninsular Italy.
wars.summary: War with Tarentum and its champion Pyrrhus of Epirus, who won costly victories at Heraclea (280) and Ausculum (279), campaigned in Sicily against Carthage (278-276) and was checked at Beneventum (275).
wars.detail: Rome's first war against a Hellenistic army, elephants and a great general. Rome refused to negotiate (Appius Claudius' speech), and no Latin colony defected. Rome and Carthage renewed their treaty (279) against Pyrrhus. The war brought Rome into the Greek world: embassies from Ptolemy II (273), the absorption of the Italiote cities as naval allies, and direct contact with Sicily that led to the First Punic War nine years later.

phases.t: Thurii; Tarentine attack on the Roman squadron; Pyrrhus invited
Heraclea; march on Rome; embassies; Ausculum
Pyrrhus in Sicily; Romans recover southern Italy piecemeal
Beneventum; Pyrrhus leaves; fall of Tarentum

scholarship: Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)

wars.name: Picene War
wars.outcome: Picenum annexed; part of the Picentes deported to the Gulf of Salerno; Latin colony at Ariminum (268).
wars.summary: Short war with the Picentes of the central Adriatic, Rome's allies since 299, ending in their defeat near Asculum during an earthquake.
wars.detail: Together with the Sallentine (267-266) and Umbrian (266) campaigns, the war completed Rome's control of peninsular Italy.

phases.t: Campaign and battle near Asculum

wars.name: Volsinian War
wars.outcome: Volsinii destroyed and refounded on Lake Bolsena; some 2,000 statues taken to Rome.
wars.summary: Roman intervention at Volsinii on behalf of its expelled aristocracy against former slaves or freedmen who had seized power, ending Etruscan independence on the eve of the First Punic War.
wars.detail: The consul Q. Fabius Gurges died of wounds in 265; M. Fulvius Flaccus took the city and triumphed in 264.

phases.t: Siege and destruction

campaigns.name: Lars Porsenna's march on Rome
campaigns.summary: Porsenna's army from Clusium came down the Chiana and Tiber valleys, seized the Janiculum and blockaded (or took) Rome; his son Arruns later pushed into Latium and was destroyed at Aricia.

path.t: Past Volsinii into the Tiber valley
Down the Tiber through Faliscan country

path.note: Veii regains the Septem Pagi under the peace

campaigns.note: Route reconstructed from geography; sources give only endpoints.

campaigns.name: Coriolanus' Volscian campaign
campaigns.summary: Livy's list of the towns Coriolanus took on his march from Volscian country to the edge of Rome: Circeii, Satricum, Longula, Polusca, Corioli, Lavinium, then Corbio, Vetelia, Trebium, Labici and Pedum, before he camped at the Fossae Cluiliae.

path.t: Antium, Volscian base of Attius Tullius

path.note: Veturia and Volumnia persuade him to withdraw

campaigns.note: The list of towns may reflect real 5th-century Volscian conquests attached to a legendary figure.

campaigns.name: The Gallic march on Rome
campaigns.summary: The Senones crossed the Apennines from the Adriatic, besieged Clusium, then marched down the Tiber valley, routed the Romans at the Allia and sacked Rome; after seven months they departed with a ransom.

path.t: Down the Paglia and Tiber valleys
Sack of Rome; siege of the Capitol

path.note: Polybius: the Veneti had invaded their lands

campaigns.note: Varronian date 390; Polybius 387/386. Diodorus has the Gauls camp in Iapygia/Apulia after the sack; Strabo says Caere defeated them on their return.

campaigns.name: The Caudine Forks campaign
campaigns.summary: The consuls concentrated at Calatia and, believing false reports that Luceria was besieged, took the short route through the Caudine pass toward Apulia, where Gavius Pontius trapped and forced the surrender of the whole army.

path.note: Samnite soldiers disguised as shepherds report Luceria under siege

path.t: Caudine Forks: army trapped and surrenders

path.note: Campanians give them clothing and arms

campaigns.note: Exact site of the Forks disputed (Arpaia-Montesarchio valley most favoured).

campaigns.name: Fabius Rullianus through the Ciminian forest
campaigns.strength: consular army, c. two legions plus allies
campaigns.summary: From Sutrium Fabius crossed the dense Ciminian forest by night, ravaged the untouched plains of central Etruria, defeated the Etruscans and brought Perusia, Cortona and Arretium to seek a truce.

path.t: Night march through the Ciminian forest
Ravaging the plains of central Etruria
Through the Chiana valley toward the northern cities

campaigns.note: Livy gives few topographical details beyond the forest and Perusia.

campaigns.name: The Sentinum campaign
campaigns.strength: four legions plus at least as many allies, c. 36,000-40,000
campaigns.summary: After a legion was destroyed near Camerinum, the consuls Fabius and Decius marched north through Umbria and crossed the Apennines to meet the Samnites and Senones at Sentinum, while diversionary attacks on Etruria drew off the Etruscans and Umbrians.
campaigns.note: Route inferred; Livy places the legion's destruction near Clusium, Polybius near Camerinum.

campaigns.name: Pyrrhus' Italian campaigns of 280-279
campaigns.strength: 20,000 foot, 3,000 horse, 2,000 archers, 500 slingers, 20 elephants (Plutarch), plus Tarentine and Italian allies
campaigns.summary: Pyrrhus crossed from Epirus, lost ships in a storm, won at Heraclea, marched up through Campania toward Rome as far as Anagnia or Praeneste, wintered at Tarentum and fought the costly victory at Ausculum in 279.

path.t: Storm-scattered landing on the Messapian coast
Battle of Heraclea on the Siris

campaigns.note: Plutarch says he came within 300 stades of Rome; Eutropius and Florus name Praeneste.

campaigns.name: Pyrrhus in Sicily and his last Italian campaign (278-275)
campaigns.strength: c. 8,000 foot and elephants crossing to Sicily; 30,000 foot and 2,500 horse with Sicilian allies (Diodorus)
campaigns.summary: Pyrrhus crossed to Sicily, relieved Syracuse, swept the Carthaginians from all but Lilybaeum, failed to take it, lost Greek support, fought his way back to Italy through a Punic fleet, was checked at Beneventum and sailed home.

path.t: Back to Syracuse amid Greek disaffection
Naval defeat in the Strait of Messina

campaigns.note: Sicilian chronology follows Diodorus 22 and Plutarch 22-24.

campaigns.name: Alexander of Epirus in southern Italy
campaigns.strength: unknown; Epirote army with Tarentine support
campaigns.summary: Invited by Tarentum, Alexander campaigned against Messapians, Lucanians, Samnites and Bruttians, from Sipontum in Apulia to Paestum and Consentia, before being killed at Pandosia.

path.t: Victory near Paestum over Samnites and Lucanians

campaigns.note: Order of operations uncertain; Livy 8.17 and 8.24 and Justin 12.2 are brief.

polities.name: Fidenae
polities.summary: Latin-Etruscan town on the left bank of the Tiber 8 km north of Rome, controlling the river crossing and the salt route; tied to Veii, it repeatedly revolted against Rome and was destroyed in 426.

polities.name: Falisci (Falerii)
polities.summary: Latin-related, Etruscan-influenced people of the middle Tiber valley with capital at Falerii Veteres (Civita Castellana); allies of Veii, they fought Rome intermittently until Falerii was destroyed in 241.

polities.name: Capena
polities.summary: Faliscan-Sabine town east of Veii, near the sanctuary of Lucus Feroniae, which aided Veii and surrendered to Rome in 395.

polities.name: Cumae
polities.summary: Oldest Greek colony in the western Mediterranean (Euboean), seat of the Sibyl; defeated the Etruscans at Aricia (c. 504) and, with Syracuse, at sea (474); taken by the Oscan Campanians in 421.

polities.name: Praeneste
polities.summary: Powerful Latin city (Palestrina) with a large territory and dependent towns, rival of Rome in the 4th century; deprived of land in 338 but remained an ally until the Social War.

polities.name: Tibur
polities.summary: Latin city (Tivoli) above the Anio falls, frequently at war with Rome in the 4th century; lost territory in 338 and remained an allied state.

polities.name: Aurunci and Ausones
polities.summary: Oscan-related peoples of the lower Liris and the Roccamonfina massif (Suessa, Cales, Ausona, Minturnae, Vescia); conquered by Rome between 345 and 314, when the Ausonian towns were destroyed.

polities.name: Sidicini
polities.summary: Oscan people centred on Teanum Sidicinum in northern Campania; Samnite attacks on them triggered the First Samnite War (343) and they fought with the Latins in 340.

polities.name: Frentani
polities.summary: Oscan-speaking people of the Adriatic coast between the Sangro and Biferno, related to the Samnites; Roman allies from 304.

polities.name: Perusia
polities.summary: Northern Etruscan city (Perugia) on a hill above the Tiber; fought Rome in 310-308 and 295, then became an allied state.

polities.name: Arretium
polities.summary: Etruscan city (Arezzo) in the upper Arno valley, Roman ally from the late 4th century, besieged by the Senones in 284.

polities.name: Thurii
polities.summary: Panhellenic colony founded under Athenian sponsorship (444/443) near the ruins of Sybaris; its appeal to Rome against the Lucanians in 282 helped provoke the Pyrrhic War.

polities.name: Rhegium
polities.summary: Chalcidian colony on the Strait of Messina (Reggio Calabria); taken by Dionysius I in 387; seized by a mutinous Campanian legion of Rome in 280 and restored to its citizens by Rome in 270.

polities.name: Mamertines (Messana)
polities.summary: Campanian mercenaries of Agathocles who seized Messana c. 288 and called themselves Mamertini, 'sons of Mars'; their appeal to Rome in 264 started the First Punic War.

series.title: Roman census figures, 5th-3rd centuries BC
series.note: From Livy and the Periochae. Fifth-century figures are generally regarded as unreliable or inflated; those from 293 onward are broadly accepted. Servius Tullius' legendary 80,000 (Livy 1.44, citing Fabius Pictor) is omitted.
